mainTopic: Acquiring from a גוי: why the Torah says ״לעמיתך״, and the ברייתא about finding an idol among purchased vessels
overview: This amud opens by finishing a derivation: just as a Jew acquires from a fellow Jew with only one method, he acquires from a גוי with only one method, which is money. The גמרא then tests אמימר, who says משיכה acquires from a גוי. His view fits רבי יוחנן, but under ריש לקיש the word ״לעמיתך״ seems extra. The גמרא first suggests the word teaches about אונאה, and then shows that one word leaves out a גוי and the other leaves out הקדש. It adds that anyone who permits robbing a גוי must hold like רבי יוחנן. Next, a ברייתא about buying broken vessels from גוים and finding an idol among them is used to challenge the view that money acquires from a גוי. The גמרא answers that the גוי accepted Jewish law, which leads to a debate between אביי and רבא about מקח טעות. רב אשי and רבינא then each offer their own reading of the ברייתא. רבינא explains that backing out of a spoken deal with a גוי is not מחוסרי אמנה.

steps.title: Just one act of acquisition for a gentile too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an earlier derivation. A Jew acquires from a fellow Jew with one method, so he also acquires from a גוי with only one method.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as with 'your counterpart' only one method works, so too with a גוי only one method works.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up a comparison from earlier on the daf. Buying from a גוי works through just one act of acquisition, the same as buying from a fellow Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison is about how many methods work, not which one. According to this view, buying from a fellow Jew uses one method (משיכה), and buying from a גוי also uses only one method (money), not both.

keyTerms.meaning: Your counterpart, meaning a fellow Jew (from the פסוק about buying and selling)
So too... also. Words used to build a comparison

phrases.english: Just as with "your counterpart" it is through one method,
phrases.notes: With a fellow Jew, this view holds that only one act works, which is pulling.

phrases.english: so too with a gentile it is also through one method.
phrases.notes: For a גוי that one method is paying money, not pulling as well.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה ״עֲמִיתֶךָ״ בְּאַחַת, אַף גּוֹי נָמֵי בְּאַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a derivation that began on the previous amud.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Acquiring from a גוי works through only one method, just like acquiring from a fellow Jew.

steps.title: אמימר's view works well if he follows רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings up אמימר, who says משיכה acquires from a גוי. That fits well if he holds like רבי יוחנן, because then ״לעמיתך״ teaches that a Jew uses money and a גוי uses משיכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to אמימר, who says pulling acquires from a גוי, this is fine if he holds like רבי יוחנן. רבי יוחנן says that by Torah law money acquires and pulling does not. Then ״לעמיתך״ has a job: with a fellow Jew you acquire by money, and with a גוי by pulling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a question on אמימר. It first shows the case where his view has no problem, so that the next step can raise the case where it does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If by Torah law money is what acquires (רבי יוחנן), the word ״לעמיתך״ tells us that money is limited to a fellow Jew. That leaves משיכה as the way to acquire from a גוי, which fits אמימר exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: Pulling an item toward yourself, a way of acquiring movable property
This works out fine (used to set up a 'but what about...' question)
It is useful, it has a purpose

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two arguments. Here the question is only about what the Torah itself says. רבי יוחנן agrees that in practice the חכמים made משיכה the way to buy between Jews, but by Torah law money works.

phrases.english: They said:
And according to Ameimar, who says
that pulling acquires with a gentile,
this works out well if he holds
like Rabbi Yochanan, who says:
by Torah law, money acquires,
pulling does not,
then "to your counterpart" has a purpose:
phrases.notes: This is the word from ויקרא 25:14, ״וכי תמכרו ממכר לעמיתך״.

phrases.english: with your counterpart by money, with a gentile by pulling.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְאָמֵימָר דְּאָמַר מְשִׁיכָה בְּגוֹי קוֹנָה, הָנִיחָא אִי סָבַר לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the previous view to אמימר's opposite view and starts testing it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If money acquires by Torah law, ״לעמיתך״ limits money to a fellow Jew, so a גוי acquires by משיכה.

steps.title: But if אמימר follows ריש לקיש, the word seems extra
steps.stepSummary: If אמימר holds like ריש לקיש that משיכה is written in the Torah, then משיכה works for both a Jew and a גוי. So why does the Torah need ״לעמיתך״?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he holds like ריש לקיש, who says pulling is stated in the Torah, then with a fellow Jew it is by pulling and with a גוי it is by pulling. So why do I need the word ״לעמיתך״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks its question. Under ריש לקיש's view, the word ״לעמיתך״ seems to have no job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If משיכה is the Torah's method for everyone, there is no difference between a Jew and a גוי in how you acquire. The word ״לעמיתך״ was supposed to mark that difference, so now it looks unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (asking why a word is written)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ,
phrases.english: But if he holds like Reish Lakish,
who says: pulling is stated clearly in the Torah,
then with your counterpart it is by pulling, and with a gentile it is by pulling,
so why do I need "to your counterpart"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the 'this works, but what about...' question set up in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: אמימר's view (משיכה acquires from a גוי), if he holds like ריש לקיש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If משיכה works for both a Jew and a גוי, the word ״לעמיתך״ does not separate them, so it seems to have no purpose.

steps.title: The word teaches that overcharge is returned only to a fellow Jew
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that ״לעמיתך״ is not about how you acquire. It teaches that you must return אונאה to a fellow Jew but not to a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: to your fellow Jew you return the overcharge, but you do not return the overcharge to a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers an answer. It gives ״לעמיתך״ a new job that has nothing to do with acquisition, about returning overcharge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק continues ״אל תונו איש את אחיו״, which is about overcharging. The answer reads ״לעמיתך״ as limiting that law to a fellow Jew, so the word has a purpose again.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying (a price unfairly off from the market value)

phrases.english: They said:
to your counterpart you return the overcharge,
but you do not return the overcharge to a gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: לַעֲמִיתֶךָ אַתָּה מַחְזִיר אוֹנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by giving ״לעמיתך״ a different purpose.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the word a different teaching (a law about overcharging instead of acquisition)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״לעמיתך״ must be teaching something about how to acquire, and under ריש לקיש it teaches nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״לעמיתך״ teaches that אונאה is returned only to a fellow Jew.

steps.title: That rule already comes from 'his brother'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer. We already know that אונאה is not returned to a גוי from the words ״איש את אחיו״, so ״לעמיתך״ is still unneeded.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rule about a גוי already comes from ״אל תונו איש את אחיו״, 'a man shall not wrong his brother'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 4. That law is already taught by another part of the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״אחיו״ (his brother) already limits the law of אונאה to a fellow Jew. So ״לעמיתך״ is not needed for that, and the original question of step 3 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A man shall not wrong his brother' (ויקרא 25:14)
It comes out from, it is learned from

steps.whyThisMatters: Because this answer falls, the question on אמימר (if he holds like ריש לקיש) comes back. The next step answers it by giving each word its own job.

phrases.aramaic: לְגוֹי — מֵ״אַל תּוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו״ נָפְקָא!
phrases.english: About a gentile, that is already learned from "A man shall not wrong his brother"!
phrases.notes: A גוי is not 'his brother,' so these words already leave him out of the law of overcharge.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְגוֹי — מֵ״אַל תּוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו״ נָפְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that ״לעמיתך״ is needed to teach the law of אונאה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That law is already learned from ״אחיו״, so it cannot be the reason ״לעמיתך״ is written.

steps.title: One verse for a non-Jew, one for consecrated property
steps.stepSummary: The two verse-words each teach something different: one leaves a גוי out of אונאה, and the other leaves הקדש out of אונאה. Both are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: One verse leaves out a גוי, and one leaves out הקדש. Both are needed. If the Torah had written only one, I would think only a גוי has no אונאה, but הקדש does. So the Torah teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from Step 5 by giving each verse-word its own job: one leaves out a גוי, the other leaves out הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 claimed ״לעמיתך״ was unneeded because ״איש את אחיו״ already leaves out a גוי. Now the גמרא says the two words are not doing the same job. Without the second word, we would think the laws of אונאה still apply to הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: Property that belongs to the בית המקדש
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: One is for a gentile, and one is for consecrated property,
phrases.notes: The two verse-words from the last step split the job: one leaves out a גוי, the other leaves out הקדש.

phrases.english: and both are needed,
for if the Torah had written only one,
I would have said:
it is a gentile who has no law of overcharging,
but consecrated property does have the law of overcharging,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַד בְּגוֹי, וְחַד בְּהֶקְדֵּשׁ, וּצְרִיכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 5 by giving the two verse-words separate jobs.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting two verses into two separate teachings (צריכותא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only one word is needed, because both words leave out a גוי.
steps.terutzMaskana: One word leaves out a גוי and the other leaves out הקדש, so both words are needed.

steps.title: Does the answer work if robbing a non-Jew is permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The answer works if robbing a גוי is forbidden. But if it is permitted, why would we need a verse to allow overcharging him?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says robbing a גוי is forbidden, because then a verse is needed to allow overcharging him. But if אמימר holds that robbing a גוי is permitted, do we even need to be told that overcharging him is allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 6. If stealing from a גוי is allowed, then overcharging him is surely allowed, and no verse is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Overcharging is a smaller wrong than outright robbery. If robbery from a גוי is permitted, a verse that only allows overcharging teaches nothing new. So the verse would be unneeded again.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it even a question? (it is obvious)

phrases.english: This works for the one who says robbing him is forbidden;
that is why a verse is needed to permit overcharging.
But if he holds
phrases.notes: "He" means אמימר, whose view we have been explaining since Step 2.

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ שֶׁל גּוֹי מוּתָּר,
phrases.english: like the one who says robbing a gentile is permitted,
is overcharging even a question?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether Step 6's answer works under every view of robbing a גוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a verse is needed to leave out a גוי from אונאה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If robbing a גוי is permitted, overcharging him is obviously permitted, so no verse is needed for it.

steps.title: Then he must hold like רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: If אמימר holds that robbing a גוי is permitted, then he must hold like רבי יוחנן, and the problem goes away.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: if he holds like the one who says robbing a גוי is permitted, you are forced to say he holds like רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and answers it: a person who permits robbing a גוי must hold like רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי יוחנן, ״לעמיתך״ does not have to teach about אונאה at all. As Step 2 explained, it teaches that a Jew buys from a Jew with money and from a גוי with משיכה. So ״לעמיתך״ has a job, and the question disappears.
steps.whatToRemember: Whoever permits robbing a גוי must hold like רבי יוחנן, so ״לעמיתך״ teaches how one acquires from a גוי.

phrases.english: They said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ מוּתָּר —
phrases.english: If he holds like the one who says robbing him is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: עַל כּוּרְחָיךְ כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: you are forced to say he holds like Rabbi Yochanan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִי סָבַר לַהּ כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר גְּזֵילוֹ מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 by tying the opinion that robbing a גוי is permitted to רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אמימר might permit robbing a גוי and also hold like ריש לקיש, which would leave ״לעמיתך״ unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Permitting robbery of a גוי goes together with רבי יוחנן, so ״לעמיתך״ teaches about acquiring with money versus משיכה.

steps.title: A ברייתא about buying broken vessels from non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא about someone who buys broken vessels from גוים and finds an idol among them. Whether he returns it depends on when he did משיכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: someone bought broken vessels from גוים and found an idol among them. If he pulled them before he paid, he returns it. If he pulled them after he paid, he must destroy it in the Dead Sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the idea that money acquires from a גוי. Here it only quotes the ברייתא; the next step explains the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the deal seems to be finished only when משיכה happens after payment. If he did משיכה before paying, the deal is not done and he can give the idol back. If he did משיכה after paying, the idol is his and he must destroy it.

keyTerms.meaning: He pulled (did משיכה, a way to acquire)

phrases.english: They challenged:
One who buys broken vessels from the gentiles
and found among them an idol:

phrases.aramaic: אִם עַד שֶׁלֹּא נָתַן מָעוֹת מָשַׁךְ —
phrases.english: if he pulled them before he gave the money,
he returns it;
and if he pulled them after he gave the money,
he takes the benefit to the Dead Sea.
phrases.notes: He must throw the idol away so he gets no benefit from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הַלּוֹקֵחַ גְּרוּטָאוֹת מִן הַגּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge, now aimed at the view that money acquires from a גוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that money acquires property from a גוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes the purchase depend on משיכה, which suggests money does not acquire from a גוי.

steps.title: If money acquires, why is pulling needed?
steps.stepSummary: If money acquires from a גוי, the ברייתא should not need משיכה at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say money acquires, why do I need pulling?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the problem from the ברייתא. If payment alone finished the deal, משיכה should not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the deal happens only through משיכה after payment. If money acquires from a גוי, the buyer would own the items as soon as he paid. So the ברייתא's focus on משיכה goes against the view that money acquires.

phrases.english: And if you say money acquires,
why do I need pulling?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מָעוֹת קוֹנוֹת, מְשִׁיכָה לְמָה לִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא in Step 9 is a challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that money acquires from a גוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If payment acquires, the buyer already owns the items after paying, so משיכה would make no difference.

steps.title: The non-Jew agreed to follow Jewish law
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a גוי who agreed to have the deal follow Jewish law, so משיכה is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the גוי accepted to be judged by Jewish law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא describes a special case: the גוי agreed to do business by Jewish law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally money would acquire from a גוי. In this ברייתא, though, the גוי chose Jewish rules for the deal. So the deal follows the Jewish way of buying, where משיכה matters.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?

phrases.english: Here, what case are we dealing with?
Where he accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן — שֶׁקִּיבֵּל עָלָיו לָדוּן בְּדִינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by limiting the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא describes a normal purchase from a גוי, so it shows that money does not acquire.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא describes a גוי who chose Jewish law, so משיכה is needed only in that special case.

steps.title: Then why mention money at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the deal follows Jewish law, then משיכה alone should be enough, so why does the ברייתא talk about paying?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 11. If משיכה is what counts here, the ברייתא should not care whether he paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes a difference between pulling before payment and pulling after payment. If only משיכה matters under Jewish law, payment should make no difference. So the wording of the ברייתא seems not to fit the new explanation.

phrases.english: If so, why do I need money?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מָעוֹת לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 11 using the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the גוי accepted Jewish law
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that explanation, only משיכה matters, so the ברייתא should not mention when the money was paid.

steps.title: Even after paying, only pulling finishes the deal
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means that even if he already paid, the deal depends on משיכה. If he pulled, he bought it. If not, he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: even though he paid money, if he pulled, yes, he bought it; and if he did not, no, he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא. Payment is mentioned only to teach that money alone does not finish the deal in this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mentioning payment does not mean money is required. It shows that even after paying, the buyer does not own the item without משיכה. This answers Step 12, and the explanation from Step 11 stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is about a גוי who chose Jewish law. In that case, even after he is paid, only משיכה completes the purchase, so the ברייתא does not disprove that money acquires from a גוי.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the ברייתא as saying the buyer needs both money and משיכה. Payment is mentioned only to show that money alone does not finish this deal.

phrases.english: This is what it means:
even though he gave the money,

phrases.aramaic: אִי מָשֵׁיךְ — אִין, וְאִי לָא — לָא.
phrases.english: if he pulled, yes; and if not, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנָּתַן מָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by rereading the ברייתא's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא mentions payment because payment is part of how the deal is completed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא mentions payment only to teach that even after paying, the deal is finished only by משיכה.

steps.title: The first clause now seems difficult
steps.stepSummary: If משיכה acquires, the first clause of the ברייתא, which says he returns the idol after pulling, is hard to explain.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the first clause is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 13 by pointing to the first clause of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 11 and 13 said the deal follows Jewish law, so משיכה makes the purchase. But the first clause says that if he pulled before paying, he may give the idol back to the גוי. That sounds like pulling did not make him the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if what you just said is true)
The first clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: The 'first clause' here is: he pulled before paying, so he returns the idol. The 'latter clause' is: he paid and then pulled, so he must destroy it. Keep these two cases straight for the whole section.

phrases.english: If so, the first clause is difficult!
phrases.notes: The first clause says that if he pulled before paying, he gives the idol back. So it seems pulling did not buy it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, קַשְׁיָא רֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 13 from the other clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 13 that משיכה decides the deal under Jewish law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If pulling acquires, then in the first clause the buyer already owns the idol and could not simply return it. Yet the ברייתא says he returns it.

steps.title: אביי: the first clause is a mistaken purchase
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that in the first clause the sale is cancelled as a מקח טעות, so he can return the idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: In the first clause, it is because there is a mistaken transaction.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge. Pulling did acquire, but this sale is cancelled because the buyer never meant to buy an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי keeps the idea that משיכה acquires. The idol goes back because the deal was a מקח טעות, not because pulling failed. A Jew would never knowingly buy an idol, so the sale of that item is void.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken purchase, which is void because the buyer did not know what he was getting

phrases.english: Abaye said:
The first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רֵישָׁא מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Recasts the reason for the ruling: the deal is void as a mistake, not because pulling failed to acquire.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Returning the idol shows that pulling did not acquire.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pulling did acquire, but the sale is cancelled as a מקח טעות.

steps.title: רבא: the latter clause is also a mistake
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks אביי why the latter clause would not also count as a מקח טעות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction, and in the latter clause there is no mistaken transaction?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges אביי's answer. The buyer did not want the idol in the second case either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both clauses the Jew did not know the idol was among the vessels. If ignorance makes the first sale a מקח טעות, it should do the same in the second. Then the second clause should also allow returning the idol, but it requires destroying it.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter (last) clause of a teaching

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
The first clause is because there is a mistaken transaction,
and in the latter clause there is no mistaken transaction?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: רֵישָׁא מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת, סֵיפָא לֵיכָּא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's answer from Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's use of מקח טעות to explain the first clause.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same lack of knowledge exists in both clauses. So מקח טעות cannot explain why the two rulings differ.

steps.title: רבא: the difference is how it looks
steps.stepSummary: רבא says both clauses are a מקח טעות. The difference is that once money is paid, it looks like the Jew owns an idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: Both the first and latter clauses are a mistaken transaction. In the first clause, where he did not pay the money, it does not look like an idol in the hands of a Jew. In the latter clause, where he paid the money, it looks like an idol in the hands of a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own explanation of the ברייתא to replace אביי's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא the sale is legally void in both cases. But if the Jew already paid and then hands the idol back, people would see it as if he had owned an idol and was trading it. So in the latter clause he must destroy it rather than return it.

keyTerms.meaning: In the possession of a Jew

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a ruling can come from how something looks to others, even when the deal is legally void.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
The first clause and the latter clause are a mistaken transaction,
the first clause, where he did not give the money —

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִיחְזֵי כַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּיַד יִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: it does not look like an idol in the hands of a Jew,
the latter clause, where he gave the money —
it looks like an idol in the hands of a Jew.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: רֵישָׁא וְסֵיפָא מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's rejected answer with רבא's own answer to the קשיא of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the difference between the clauses away from the law of the sale to how the situation appears.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference between the clauses must be about whether the sale is valid.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sales are mistaken. Only payment makes it look like the Jew owned an idol, which requires destroying it.

steps.title: אביי defends his answer
steps.stepSummary: אביי can reply that after paying, the buyer should have checked before pulling, so the latter clause is not a mistaken purchase.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי could say to you: The first clause is a mistaken transaction, because he did not know, since he had not yet paid him money. The latter clause is not a mistaken transaction, because once he paid, when he pulled he should have inspected and then pulled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how אביי would answer רבא's challenge from Step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before paying, a buyer has no reason to look closely yet, so not noticing the idol is a real mistake. After paying, he should have inspected the goods before pulling. If he did not bother, he accepted whatever was there, so the sale stands.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (a defense of his view)

phrases.english: And Abaye could say to you:
The first clause is a mistaken transaction, because he did not know,
since he had not given him the money.
phrases.notes: Before paying, a buyer does not check the goods closely yet, so not noticing the idol is a real mistake.

phrases.english: The latter clause is not a mistaken transaction,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֵיוָן דִּיהַיב זוּזֵי, כִּי קָא מָשֵׁיךְ —
phrases.english: because since he gave the money, when he was pulling —
he should have inspected and then pulled.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַבַּיֵּי אָמַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to אביי's view and answers רבא's challenge from Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a real difference between the two clauses: whether the buyer was expected to inspect.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses involve the same ignorance, so both are a מקח טעות.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the first clause is a מקח טעות. After paying, failing to inspect before pulling means he accepted the goods.

steps.title: רב אשי: pulling does nothing in either clause
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reads the ברייתא as following the rule that money acquires from a גוי. משיכה does nothing, and the latter clause says 'pulled' only to match the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Since in the first clause pulling does not acquire, in the latter clause too pulling does not acquire. Since the first clause taught 'pulled,' the latter clause also taught 'pulled.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי goes back to the challenge in Step 10 and answers it a different way, without saying the גוי agreed to Jewish law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 asked: if money acquires from a גוי, why does the latter clause mention pulling? רב אשי answers that the first clause already shows pulling alone does not acquire. So pulling does not count in the latter clause either; only the payment matters. The word 'pulled' there is just repeated so the two clauses sound alike.

keyTerms.meaning: Pulling an item toward oneself, a way of acquiring it
Since; because (it was already said in one place)

steps.whatToRemember: So far there are three ways to read the ברייתא. אביי: pulling acquires, but the first clause is a מקח טעות. רבא: both are a מקח טעות, but after payment it looks like a Jew owns an idol. רב אשי: money acquires from a גוי, and 'pulled' in the latter clause is only there to match the first clause. רבינא gives another reading in the next step.
steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not adding a new law about pulling. He is saying one word in the latter clause has no legal meaning. It is only there because the first clause used it.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
From the fact that in the first clause pulling does not acquire,
in the latter clause too pulling does not acquire,
and since the first clause taught "pulled,"
the latter clause also taught "pulled."
phrases.notes: The word is there only to match the first clause. It does not affect the ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: מִדְּרֵישָׁא מְשִׁיכָה אֵינָהּ קוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אביי and רבא discussion and gives a different answer to the challenge in Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the extra word as only matching the first clause, so the case does not need to be changed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mentioning 'pulled' in the latter clause shows that משיכה matters, which goes against the view that money acquires from a גוי.
steps.terutzMaskana: Money alone acquires. 'Pulled' in the latter clause is repeated only to match the first clause.

steps.title: רבינא: pulling acquires in both clauses
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the סיפא shows that מְשִׁיכָה acquires, so it acquires in the רישא too. He rereads the רישא as a case where the buyer neither paid nor pulled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Since in the latter clause pulling acquires, in the first clause pulling also acquires. The first clause means this: if he did not pay and did not pull, he may go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new way to read the ברייתא. In his reading, pulling always acquires, and the first clause is about a deal where nothing was done yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answers had to explain why pulling did not lock in the deal in the רישא. רבינא keeps the rule the same in both clauses: מְשִׁיכָה acquires. He solves the problem by changing the case of the רישא, so that nothing was paid and nothing was pulled.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause of the ברייתא
The first clause of the ברייתא
Pulling the item, a way of acquiring it
He may go back (back out of the deal)

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא does not deny that money normally acquires from a גוי. Like the earlier answer in Step 11, he reads the ברייתא as a case where the גוי accepted Jewish law, so here pulling is what acquires, in both clauses. רב אשי instead reads it as an ordinary sale, where only the money counts.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Since in the latter clause pulling acquires,
in the first clause too pulling acquires,
and the first clause is saying this:

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא נָתַן וְלֹא מָשַׁךְ — יַחְזוֹר.
phrases.english: If he did not give and did not pull, he may go back.
phrases.notes: 'Give' means paying the money; 'pull' means taking hold of the idol.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: מִדְּסֵיפָא מְשִׁיכָה קוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth answer, different from those of אביי, רבא and רב אשי.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the case of the רישא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רישא seemed to say the buyer pulled and could still return the idol, as if pulling did nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Pulling acquires in both clauses. The רישא is a case of no payment and no pulling.

steps.title: What does 'he may go back' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'יחזור' means if nothing was paid or pulled.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'he goes back' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask a clarifying question about the word 'יחזור'. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no money was paid and nothing was pulled, there is nothing physical to give back. So the word 'יחזור' needs a new meaning in רבינא's reading.

phrases.english: What does 'he goes back' mean?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי יַחְזוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word in רבינא's reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'יחזור' means when nothing was paid or pulled.

steps.title: He backs out of his words
steps.stepSummary: 'יחזור' means he may back out of his verbal agreement.
steps.simpleTranslation: He goes back on his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'he goes back' means he may cancel the spoken deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer and the גוי had only agreed in words. 'יחזור' means the Jew may back out of that agreement without finishing the purchase.

keyTerms.meaning: Words; here, a spoken agreement with no act of acquiring
Backing out of a verbal commitment

phrases.english: He goes back on words.

steps.triggerLanguage: יַחְזוֹר בִּדְבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'יחזור' means backing out of a verbal commitment.

steps.title: Why the תנא needed to say this
steps.stepSummary: The תנא holds that backing out of words is מחוסרי אמנה. But that applies only between Jews, who keep their word, not with a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that backing out of words counts as lacking trustworthiness. But that applies only to a Jew buying from a Jew, since they keep their word. A Jew buying from gentiles, who do not keep their word, is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ברייתא had to teach that the buyer may back out of words. Normally doing that is looked down upon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Backing out of a spoken deal is usually called מחוסרי אמנה. Here the seller is a גוי who is not expected to keep his word, so neither side was relying on the other's word. That is why the ברייתא teaches the Jew may freely back out.
steps.whatToRemember: רבינא: pulling acquires in both clauses. In the רישא nothing was done, and the Jew may back out of his words. That is not מחוסרי אמנה, because the seller is a גוי who does not keep his word either.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the rule of מחוסרי אמנה depends on both sides being expected to keep their word.

phrases.english: He holds:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the תנא of the ברייתא, as רבינא understands him.

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָרִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה,
phrases.english: words carry the issue of lacking trustworthiness,
and this applies only to a Jew from a Jew,
since they stand by their words,
but a Jew from gentiles,
since they do not stand by their words, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: דְּבָרִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶם מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ברייתא needed to say 'he may back out of words'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the teaching is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think backing out of a spoken deal is always wrong, so the ברייתא would not allow it.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a גוי, who does not keep his word, backing out is not מחוסרי אמנה, so the Jew may back out.
